title: Key Atlantic currents could collapse this century, but the risk is missing from almost all national climate plans
summary: Icelandic government officials recently met to discuss a dramatic scenario: what if the current that circulates Atlantic waters weakened significantly, or collapsed altogether?

Credit: Brenden Jongman / NASA and NOAA data / AMOC Icelandic government officials recently met to discuss a dramatic scenario: what if the current that circulates Atlantic waters weakened significantly, or collapsed altogether? The ocean currents are changing, with major implications for climate around the world. Yet our new article published in Nature Sustainability suggests most governments are not preparing for this possibility. Of 91 national adaptation plans submitted to the U.N. climate convention, only two even mention that key Atlantic current, and neither sets out concrete action in response to its possible collapse. The Atlantic meridional overturning circulation, or AMOC, is part of the giant conveyor belt of ocean currents that moves warm surface water northward in the Atlantic and sends colder deep water back south. It plays a critical role in regulating the global climate by redistributing heat around the planet, influencing weather patterns and temperatures far beyond the Atlantic basin. As the climate warms, the AMOC is weakening and could continue to do so throughout this century. While a full collapse, in which major ocean currents completely reorient, is unlikely before 2100, a recent study projected a 50% weakening of the AMOC by the end of the century under an intermediate emissions scenario. A collapse would not be unique in geological history. Studies show that the AMOC has undergone dramatic changes before, including a near-complete shutdown around 17,500 years ago, after the coldest period in the last ice age. The effects of an AMOC slowdown would be felt across the world. Credit: Jongman & Hall (2026), Nature Sustainability A slowdown or collapse would have major implications for temperature and rainfall around the world. In northern Europe, the loss of the heat AMOC transfers northward from the tropics could lead to winter cold extremes of -20°C (-4 degrees Fahrenheit) in London. Climate model experiments in which the AMOC is shut down show an average 29% weakening of the West African monsoons and 19% weakening of the Indian summer monsoon, increasing risks of food and water insecurity in regions that rely on monsoon rains. Other studies suggest an increased risk of severe drought in parts of Central America, West Africa and the Amazon region. Fisheries and sea level would also be affected. So how can countries prepare for changes in ocean circulation whose timing is highly uncertain? Our article identifies practical steps to incorporate AMOC-related risks into adaptation decision-making. Most investments assume only gradual change Of the 91 national adaptation plans reported to the U.N. climate convention so far, only two mention the AMOC. Brazil's plan devotes a dedicated box to warning that its shutdown could push the Atlantic rain belt southward, tipping the Amazon rainforest toward collapse. Ireland —which relies on the AMOC to sustain its mild climate—mentions that "reliance solely on adaptation may prove insufficient" in case of AMOC collapse, concluding that no national plan can prepare for such tipping points. It represents a very high-impact scenario whose likelihood is very difficult to quantify. And yet if the current were to collapse, some parts of the world could experience climate changes in the opposite direction to those they are preparing for, most notably colder winters in northwestern Europe. This is important because many adaptation investments need to be robust to a wide range of potential changes to be effective. Consider a country planning to build a new reservoir to cope with more variable rainfall amounts under climate change. If instead the rainy season becomes shorter and there is less rain overall, the reservoir may seem like a bad investment. Similarly, in countries that depend on monsoon rains, a weakening or collapse of the AMOC could mean even less rainfall than is projected under climate change. Along Atlantic coastlines, changes in sea level and ocean temperatures could affect how well coastal defenses work. Changes in fish stocks could also threaten communities that depend on fishing.
